page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard3.Flex.2-32 is a flexible virtual machine instance built on the x86_64 architecture and powered by an Intel Xeon 8358 processor running at a base clock speed of 2.6 GHz. The hardware profile is provisioned with 2 physical cores and 4 dedicated vCPUs, utilizing two threads per core. System memory is sized at 32.0 GB, yielding a high ratio of 8.0 GB of memory per vCPU.

This server type does not feature bundled local storage, requiring workloads to rely on remote block storage or network file systems for persistent data. The instance configuration contains zero discrete GPUs. Network connectivity comes with one complimentary public IPv4 address. From a resource-efficiency standpoint, the 1:8 vCPU-to-memory allocation allows memory-dense applications to run efficiently without requiring the purchase of surplus compute cores, though workloads with high I/O throughput must factor in the latency of attached network volumes.

Given its combination of dedicated Intel compute resources and an elevated memory capacity, VM.Standard3.Flex.2-32 is appropriate for running memory-resident databases, caching layers such as Redis, enterprise backend applications, and data pre-processing jobs that require substantial working memory relative to compute threads.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard3.Flex.2-32 is an x86_64 virtual machine powered by an Intel Xeon 8358 processor running at 2.6 GHz. It is provisioned with 2 physical cores that deliver 4 dedicated vCPUs alongside 32.0 GB of system memory. Delivering 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU, this instance features a 1:8 compute-to-memory ratio designed to accommodate memory-heavy processes without necessitating excessive CPU allocations. The configuration includes no local storage, requiring network-attached storage solutions for disk operations, and contains no hardware accelerators. A single complimentary public IPv4 address is included. VM.Standard3.Flex.2-32 is suited for memory-intensive operational workloads, including relational database engines, in-memory caches, middleware, and enterprise backends that prioritize dedicated memory density over high core counts.
